categories.title: RAG Pipeline Decisions
categories.subtitle: Knowledge Bases, vector stores, chunking, embedding, and retrieval quality

decisionPatterns.scenario: A law firm's RAG app splits contract clauses across chunks because provisions span multiple paragraphs and reference other sections.
decisionPatterns.why: Preserves the parent-child structure of document sections so multi-paragraph clauses stay intact as complete units.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A company's knowledge base covers 50 products, but search results for Product A keep returning docs from Product B because they share similar terminology.
decisionPatterns.why: Pre-filters vector search by product or category tag before semantic matching, so only the correct product's documents are considered.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A pharma company's RAG search misunderstands specialized drug names and chemical terminology because the embedding model was trained on general web text.
decisionPatterns.why: An embedding model trained on scientific/medical text produces more meaningful vectors for specialized terminology than a generic model with more dimensions.

decisionPatterns.scenario: Users complain the knowledge base still shows yesterday's product specs even though the S3 source documents were updated this morning.
decisionPatterns.why: Bedrock Knowledge Bases don't auto-sync — you must trigger an ingestion job (or schedule one) to re-embed updated documents into the vector store.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A RAG app retrieves the correct FDA drug documents, but the model's summary includes a drug interaction warning that doesn't appear anywhere in the source material.
decisionPatterns.why: Verifies each claim in the model's response against the retrieved source documents and blocks statements that aren't supported by the reference material.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A medical GenAI app sometimes invents plausible-sounding but incorrect treatment recommendations, which could endanger patient safety.
decisionPatterns.why: RAG grounds responses in verified source data; grounding checks verify the model stayed faithful to that data. Two complementary layers for safety-critical applications.

services.name: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
services.whatItDoes: Managed RAG service: handles chunking, embedding, vector indexing, and retrieval from S3 data sources
whenNotToChoose: Need full control over embedding pipeline
commonTraps: KB does NOT auto-sync when S3 documents change -- you must trigger StartIngestionJob
Embedding model version changes cause silent retrieval degradation (vector drift)

services.name: Hierarchical Chunking
services.whatItDoes: Chunking strategy that preserves document structure (sections, subsections, clauses) instead of splitting at arbitrary character boundaries
whenToChoose: Any structured document where context spans paragraphs
whenNotToChoose: Simple, flat text like FAQs or product descriptions
commonTraps: Thinking bigger fixed chunks solve structure problems -- they add noise without preserving relationships
Confusing chunk size tuning with chunking strategy changes

services.name: Metadata Filtering
services.whatItDoes: Pre-filters vector search by metadata tags (product, category, department) before semantic similarity is evaluated
whenNotToChoose: When the problem is relevance ranking, not wrong-category results
commonTraps: Increasing top-K to solve precision problems -- that increases recall, not precision

services.name: Contextual Grounding Checks (Guardrails)
services.whatItDoes: Verifies that each claim in the model's response is supported by the provided reference context; flags or blocks ungrounded claims
whenToChoose: RAG applications where faithfulness to source material is critical
commonTraps: Confusing contextual grounding (factual faithfulness) with content filters (safety/harmful content)

categories.title: Guardrails: Which Filter Type?
categories.subtitle: Content filters vs denied topics vs word filters vs PII filters vs grounding checks

decisionPatterns.scenario: A chatbot occasionally generates responses containing hate speech or violent language that violates company policy.
decisionPatterns.why: Blocks harmful content categories (hate, violence, sexual, misconduct) with configurable severity thresholds on both inputs and outputs.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A financial chatbot must never provide investment recommendations or tax advice, regardless of how creatively users phrase their requests.
decisionPatterns.why: Uses natural language descriptions to detect prohibited business topics semantically — understands intent even when users rephrase to avoid specific keywords.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A company wants to block specific competitor brand names and profanity from ever appearing in chatbot responses.
decisionPatterns.why: Exact keyword/phrase matching that blocks specific strings. Simple and precise for known words, but won't catch rephrased versions.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A healthcare app must ensure Social Security numbers, phone numbers, and emails never appear in model outputs — and adding new PII types shouldn't require code changes.
decisionPatterns.why: Auto-detects and blocks built-in PII types in outputs. New PII types are added via configuration, not code — meeting compliance without deployment cycles.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A compliance team needs to know which specific guardrail policy (content filter, denied topic, or PII filter) blocked a particular response.
decisionPatterns.why: Shows which policy category triggered the block. The GuardrailContentSource dimension only tells you input vs output — not which policy fired.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A security team needs to ensure every Bedrock API call across the organization must pass through a specific guardrail — no exceptions.
decisionPatterns.why: Attaches a condition to InvokeModel IAM policies requiring a specific guardrail ID, making it impossible to invoke models without the guardrail.

services.name: Content Filters
services.whatItDoes: Blocks harmful content categories (hate, violence, sexual, misconduct) with configurable severity thresholds for both input and output
whenToChoose: Need to block harmful content categories
commonTraps: Using content filters to block business topics like 'investment advice' -- that's a denied topic, not a harmful content category

services.name: Denied Topics
services.whatItDoes: Uses natural language descriptions to define prohibited business topics; understands semantic intent regardless of phrasing
whenToChoose: Topics that users might rephrase creatively
commonTraps: Using word filters for topic blocking -- users will rephrase to bypass keywords

services.name: Sensitive Information Filters (PII)
services.whatItDoes: Auto-detects and blocks/masks PII types (SSNs, emails, phone numbers, addresses) in inputs and outputs without custom code
whenToChoose: Need configurable PII types without code changes
whenNotToChoose: Custom data formats not covered by built-in PII types
commonTraps: Building custom Lambda regex for PII when Guardrails provides this natively
Relying on system prompt to prevent PII -- models can be jailbroken

services.name: Contextual Grounding Checks
services.whatItDoes: Evaluates whether each claim in the response is supported by provided reference context; flags or blocks ungrounded claims
whenToChoose: RAG applications where source faithfulness is critical
Model adds information beyond retrieved documents
commonTraps: Confusing grounding checks (factual verification) with content filters (safety moderation)

categories.title: Model Customization Escalation Path
categories.subtitle: Right-sizing, prompting, fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and distillation

decisionPatterns.scenario: A startup's chatbot handles simple order-status queries and return policies — no complex reasoning needed, but responses must be under 500ms on a tight budget.
decisionPatterns.why: Simple tasks don't need large models. A smaller FM is faster and cheaper per token — right-sizing to the task saves both latency and cost.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A sentiment classifier works well on obvious reviews but misclassifies sarcastic ones. The team can't fine-tune but has examples of sarcastic reviews with correct labels.
decisionPatterns.why: Providing labeled examples of the edge cases in the prompt teaches the model the pattern in-context without requiring training infrastructure.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A model keeps getting multi-step math problems wrong because it jumps straight to the answer without working through intermediate calculations.
decisionPatterns.why: Instructing the model to 'show step-by-step reasoning' forces it to work through intermediate logic, catching errors before the final answer.

decisionPatterns.scenario: Few-shot prompting plateaued at 73% accuracy for extracting medication data from doctor's notes into JSON. The team has 200 labeled examples and needs 95%+.
decisionPatterns.why: When prompting hits a ceiling and you have labeled input→output pairs, fine-tuning teaches the model the exact extraction patterns. It also eliminates the token overhead of few-shot examples in every request.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A genomics FM performs poorly on proprietary research terminology. The company has 50,000 unlabeled research papers but no labeled question-answer pairs.
decisionPatterns.why: Exposes the FM to the unlabeled domain corpus so it learns specialized vocabulary and concepts. Unlike fine-tuning, CPT doesn't require labeled data.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A company sends 2 million templated email replies per month using a large FM. The replies follow predictable patterns and the cost is unsustainable.
decisionPatterns.why: Creates a smaller, cheaper model optimized for this narrow task by learning from the larger teacher model. Dramatically reduces per-invocation cost at high volume.

services.name: Few-Shot Prompting
services.whatItDoes: Provides examples of desired input-output behavior in the prompt so the model learns the pattern in-context
whenToChoose: Model fails on specific edge cases
whenNotToChoose: Accuracy plateau (>10 examples with no improvement)
Context window too small for examples + input
commonTraps: Adding more examples indefinitely -- diminishing returns after ~5-10 examples

services.name: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
services.whatItDoes: Instructs the model to break reasoning into explicit intermediate steps before giving a final answer
commonTraps: Thinking temperature 0 fixes reasoning -- it makes errors consistent, not correct

services.name: Fine-Tuning (Amazon Bedrock)
services.whatItDoes: Trains the FM on labeled input-output pairs to learn task-specific behavior and output formats
whenToChoose: Prompt engineering plateaus below required accuracy
whenNotToChoose: No labeled data available (use continued pre-training)
commonTraps: Jumping to fine-tuning before trying prompt engineering (always try prompts first)
Confusing with continued pre-training (fine-tuning = labeled, CPT = unlabeled)

services.name: Continued Pre-Training (Amazon Bedrock)
services.whatItDoes: Exposes the FM to a large unlabeled domain corpus so it learns domain vocabulary, terminology, and concepts
whenToChoose: Specialized terminology the base model doesn't understand
whenNotToChoose: Have labeled data and need task-specific behavior (use fine-tuning)
Problem is task format, not domain knowledge
commonTraps: Confusing CPT (unlabeled, learns knowledge) with fine-tuning (labeled, learns behavior)

services.name: Model Distillation (Amazon Bedrock)
services.whatItDoes: Creates a smaller, cheaper model optimized for a specific task by learning from a larger teacher model
whenToChoose: Cost is primary concern at scale
whenNotToChoose: Complex reasoning tasks requiring full model capability
Low volume where cost savings are minimal
commonTraps: Using full-size FMs for narrow tasks at high volume -- massive cost waste

categories.title: Throughput & Cost Optimization
categories.subtitle: Cross-Region inference, Provisioned Throughput, batch inference, prompt caching

decisionPatterns.scenario: An app gets 'Too many requests' throttling errors from Bedrock during peak hours but needs to keep using the same FM without adding infrastructure.
decisionPatterns.why: Automatically distributes requests to Regions with available capacity. Same FM, same API, no operational overhead — just more throughput during peaks.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A marketing team needs to generate personalized emails for 500,000 customers. Results are needed within 24 hours, and cost must be minimized.
decisionPatterns.why: Processes large request volumes asynchronously at a discounted rate compared to on-demand. Perfect for non-real-time, high-volume jobs.

decisionPatterns.scenario: Every API call to Bedrock includes the same 5,000-token system prompt with company policies. The team wants to reduce both cost and latency for these repeated tokens.
decisionPatterns.why: Caches static prompt components across requests so those tokens aren't reprocessed each time — reducing both per-request cost and first-token latency.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A European company must comply with GDPR and ensure all Bedrock data processing stays within the EU.
decisionPatterns.why: AWS Regions are physically isolated — deploying in eu-west-1 or eu-central-1 keeps all processing in the EU. Cross-Region inference must be disabled because it may route to non-EU Regions.

services.name: Cross-Region Inference
services.whatItDoes: Automatically routes Bedrock requests to Regions with available capacity, increasing throughput during peak periods
whenNotToChoose: Need to control which Region processes data
commonTraps: Enabling cross-Region inference when GDPR requires data to stay in a specific Region

services.name: Batch Inference
services.whatItDoes: Processes large volumes of FM requests asynchronously at a discounted per-request rate
commonTraps: Thinking parallel Lambda reduces per-request cost -- it only reduces wall-clock time, same price

services.name: Prompt Caching
services.whatItDoes: Caches static prompt components (system prompts, few-shot examples) across requests so cached tokens aren't reprocessed
whenToChoose: Large system prompts repeated on every call
High request volume with shared context
whenNotToChoose: Every prompt is unique with no shared components
commonTraps: Using RAG for static system prompt content (RAG is for dynamic retrieval, not static context)

services.name: Provisioned Throughput
services.whatItDoes: Reserves dedicated model capacity for consistent throughput guarantees regardless of demand
whenNotToChoose: Spiky traffic (pay for capacity you don't use)
commonTraps: Thinking Provisioned Throughput reduces per-request latency -- it guarantees capacity, not speed

categories.title: Agent Architecture Patterns
categories.subtitle: Agents, Action Groups, ROC, multi-agent, Flows, Converse API tool use

decisionPatterns.scenario: An AI assistant needs to autonomously check inventory, update shipping status, and calculate delivery estimates by calling the company's internal REST APIs.
decisionPatterns.why: Action Groups define available API operations via OpenAPI schemas. The agent decides which to call based on user intent, and Lambda executes the actual API calls.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A banking agent processes fund transfers, but regulations require the user to explicitly confirm transfer details before the agent executes the transaction.
decisionPatterns.why: Pauses agent execution after determining the action parameters but before executing. Returns the proposed action to the application so it can present details to the user and wait for confirmation.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A travel planning chatbot needs to remember the customer's destination, dates, and hotel preferences mentioned 30 turns ago in the same conversation.
decisionPatterns.why: Passing the same sessionId with each InvokeAgent call maintains conversation history natively. No need for custom DynamoDB session storage.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A customer service system has separate specialist agents for orders, recommendations, and complaints — a supervisor must route each request to the right specialist.
decisionPatterns.why: A supervisor agent dynamically routes to specialized sub-agents, each with their own instructions, tools, and knowledge bases. The supervisor coordinates and synthesizes results.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A developer needs to build a document processing pipeline: extract text with Textract, summarize with an FM, classify the document type, and store results — using a visual drag-and-drop interface.
decisionPatterns.why: Visual, low-code workflow builder for predefined multi-step GenAI pipelines. Different from Agents (which are autonomous and conversational) — Flows are for structured, sequential processing.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A Converse API application needs the model to check real-time weather data and do currency conversions during a chat, deciding when to use each tool.
decisionPatterns.why: Define tool specifications in the Converse API request. The model requests tool invocations, your code executes them, and you return results in the next turn. Developer-managed, not a separate agent service.

services.name: Amazon Bedrock Agents
services.whatItDoes: Autonomous AI agents that use ReAct-style orchestration to decide which actions to take based on user intent, executing via Action Groups
whenToChoose: Need to call external APIs based on user intent
whenNotToChoose: Simple tool use in Converse API conversations
commonTraps: Thinking FMs can make HTTP calls directly -- they generate text, not network requests; Action Groups + Lambda bridge this gap

services.name: Return of Control (ROC)
services.whatItDoes: Pauses agent execution after determining the action but before executing it; returns proposed action to the calling application for user confirmation
whenNotToChoose: Fully autonomous workflows with no confirmation needed
commonTraps: Confusing guardrails (content filtering) with ROC (workflow control) -- different purposes entirely

services.name: Multi-Agent Collaboration
services.whatItDoes: A supervisor agent dynamically routes to and coordinates multiple specialized sub-agents, each with independent instructions, tools, and knowledge bases
whenToChoose: Dynamic routing based on user intent
whenNotToChoose: When one agent with Action Groups suffices
commonTraps: Using Step Functions for dynamic AI routing -- it's for predefined workflows, not intent-based routing

services.name: Amazon Bedrock Flows
services.whatItDoes: Visual, low-code workflow builder for multi-step GenAI pipelines connecting prompts, models, knowledge bases, Lambda functions, and conditional logic
commonTraps: Confusing Flows (predefined workflows) with Agents (autonomous AI) -- different paradigms

services.name: Converse API Tool Use
services.whatItDoes: Function calling protocol in the Converse API: define tool specifications, model requests tool invocation, your code executes tools, results returned in next turn
whenToChoose: Need fine-grained control over tool execution
whenNotToChoose: Want fully managed agentic orchestration (use Bedrock Agents)
commonTraps: Confusing Converse API tool use (developer-managed) with Bedrock Agents (managed agentic service)

services.name: AgentCore SDK + Starter Toolkit
services.whatItDoes: SDK provides @app.entrypoint decorator for auto HTTP server setup; toolkit automates packaging, containerization, and deployment to AgentCore Runtime
whenToChoose: Deploying Python agents to Bedrock AgentCore
Minimal operational overhead for agent hosting
Need both JSON and streaming response support
commonTraps: Building FastAPI servers manually when AgentCore SDK auto-creates HTTP endpoints

categories.title: Observability & Logging: Which Tool When?
categories.subtitle: CloudWatch, invocation logging, CloudTrail, X-Ray, and model evaluation

decisionPatterns.scenario: An ops team needs automated Slack alerts when Bedrock error rates spike or p99 latency exceeds 3 seconds.
decisionPatterns.why: Bedrock publishes native metrics (errors, latency, token counts) to CloudWatch. Set Alarms on thresholds to trigger SNS notifications — no custom log parsing needed.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A compliance team needs the full text of every prompt and model response stored for 7 years, searchable for regulatory audits.
decisionPatterns.why: Captures complete request/response payloads and delivers to S3 for long-term retention. Query with Athena for investigations. CloudTrail only logs API metadata (who/when), not content.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A security team needs to investigate which IAM user called Bedrock at 2am last Tuesday and from which IP address.
decisionPatterns.why: Logs API call metadata: principal, timestamp, source IP, API action. It does NOT capture the prompt or response content — that's invocation logging.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A GenAI app's satisfaction scores have been slowly declining for two months, but no code, prompts, or model versions have changed.
decisionPatterns.service: Continuous Evaluation with Updated Test Datasets
decisionPatterns.why: Gradual decline without code changes usually means data/concept drift — real-world patterns have shifted. Regular evaluation against current test data detects this. CloudWatch metrics show infrastructure health, not content quality.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A developer needs to debug why a Guardrail blocked a specific response — was it a content filter, denied topic, or PII filter?
decisionPatterns.why: The GuardrailPolicyType CloudWatch dimension shows which policy category triggered. GuardrailContentSource only shows whether it was the input or output that was flagged.

services.name: Amazon CloudWatch (Bedrock Metrics)
services.whatItDoes: Bedrock publishes native metrics: InvocationCount, InvocationErrors, InvocationLatency, InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount. Use Alarms for automated alerting via SNS.
whenNotToChoose: Need full prompt/response content (use invocation logging)
commonTraps: Building custom Lambda log parsing when CloudWatch already has native Bedrock metrics

services.name: Bedrock Model Invocation Logging
services.whatItDoes: Captures complete request and response payloads (prompts and model outputs) and delivers to S3 or CloudWatch Logs
whenNotToChoose: Only need API call metadata (use CloudTrail)
commonTraps: Thinking CloudTrail captures prompt/response content -- it only logs API metadata (who, when, what API)

services.name: AWS CloudTrail
services.whatItDoes: Logs API call metadata: which IAM principal called which API, when, from which IP address. Does NOT capture request/response content.
whenNotToChoose: Need actual prompt/response content (use invocation logging)
commonTraps: Choosing CloudTrail for 'full request logging' -- it only has metadata, not content

services.name: Continuous Model Evaluation
services.whatItDoes: Periodically runs the model against updated test datasets that reflect current patterns, comparing results to baseline metrics to detect drift
whenToChoose: No code changes but satisfaction dropping
commonTraps: Looking at CloudWatch metrics (latency, errors) for content quality problems -- those are infrastructure metrics, not relevance

categories.title: Security & Access Control
categories.subtitle: IAM conditions, SCPs, PrivateLink, KMS, authentication federation

decisionPatterns.scenario: Two teams in the same AWS account need different Bedrock model access — the ML team gets Claude Opus, app teams get Haiku only.
decisionPatterns.why: Per-role IAM conditions restrict which model ARNs each role can invoke. Bedrock's account-level model access is all-or-nothing — IAM conditions provide per-team granularity.

decisionPatterns.scenario: An enterprise with 20 AWS accounts needs to prevent all accounts from using unauthorized Bedrock models, and account admins must not be able to override the restriction.
decisionPatterns.why: SCPs are organization-level permission guardrails that no account administrator can override. The only AWS mechanism that provides non-bypassable restrictions across all member accounts.

decisionPatterns.scenario: Security policy requires that all Bedrock API calls from EC2 instances in a private subnet must never traverse the public internet.
decisionPatterns.why: Creates a private connection from the VPC to Bedrock within the AWS network. NAT Gateways route through the internet gateway — that's public internet, not private.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A government agency needs vector database encryption with keys they control, rotate on schedule, and can revoke immediately if compromised.
decisionPatterns.why: The agency owns the key, sets rotation schedules, and can disable/delete it instantly. AWS-managed keys don't give the customer control over rotation or revocation.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A European company must ensure GDPR compliance — all customer data processed by Bedrock must stay within EU boundaries.
decisionPatterns.why: AWS Regions are isolated. Deploying in eu-west-1 keeps all data in the EU. Cross-Region inference must be disabled because it may route requests to non-EU Regions.

services.name: IAM Condition Keys (bedrock:ModelId)
services.whatItDoes: Restricts which Bedrock models specific IAM roles can invoke, enabling per-team model access control within the same account
whenToChoose: Per-team model restrictions in same account
Cost control by restricting expensive models
whenNotToChoose: Account-wide model enabling/disabling (use Bedrock model access management)
commonTraps: Confusing Bedrock model access management (account-level toggle) with IAM-based access control (role-level conditions)

services.name: Service Control Policies (SCPs)
services.whatItDoes: Organization-level permission guardrails that apply to all principals in all member accounts and cannot be overridden at the account level
whenToChoose: Must be non-overridable by account admins
commonTraps: Confusing Config rules (detective, after-the-fact) with SCPs (preventive, blocks before it happens)

services.name: VPC Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink)
services.whatItDoes: Creates a private connection from VPC to AWS services without traversing the public internet
whenToChoose: Security policy requires no public internet traffic
whenNotToChoose: Public-facing applications where internet routing is acceptable
commonTraps: Thinking NAT Gateway keeps traffic private -- it routes through the internet gateway (public internet)
Confusing VPN (on-premises connectivity) with PrivateLink (AWS service connectivity)

services.name: AWS KMS Customer-Managed Keys
services.whatItDoes: Customer-controlled encryption keys with key rotation scheduling, usage auditing via CloudTrail, and cross-account key sharing
whenNotToChoose: Default encryption is acceptable (use AWS-managed keys for simplicity)
commonTraps: Confusing AWS-managed keys (convenient, no customer control) with customer-managed keys (full control, rotation, audit)

categories.title: Deployment & Inference Patterns
categories.subtitle: Streaming, Converse API, inference profiles, SageMaker inference types

decisionPatterns.scenario: Users complain about staring at a blank screen for 10 seconds while the chatbot generates a long response before anything appears.
decisionPatterns.why: The streaming API returns tokens as they're generated. WebSocket (not REST) API Gateway enables pushing chunks to the browser in real-time. REST is synchronous — it can't stream partial responses.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A team maintains separate API integration code for Claude, Nova, and Llama — each with different request formats. Bugs appear when one integration is updated but others aren't.
decisionPatterns.why: Provides a unified request/response format across all models. One integration instead of three. Model-specific parameters go through additionalModelRequestFields.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A company wants to gradually migrate from Claude Sonnet to Opus, shifting 10% of traffic first and automatically rolling back if quality drops.
decisionPatterns.why: Native traffic splitting between models with a single endpoint ARN. Adjust weights to shift traffic gradually. Pair with CloudWatch Alarms for automated rollback.

decisionPatterns.scenario: An app needs to look at a product photo and generate a marketing description — understanding both the visual content and producing persuasive text.
decisionPatterns.why: Multimodal FMs accept image + text in one call. Chaining Rekognition labels + text FM loses visual nuance and adds an extra API call. One multimodal call is simpler and richer.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A SageMaker model needs to process 500MB research documents that take 12 minutes per inference, and the endpoint should scale to zero when idle.
decisionPatterns.why: Handles payloads up to 1GB and long-running inferences. Auto-scales to zero when idle. Real-Time endpoints have a 25MB limit and no scale-to-zero.

services.name: InvokeModelWithResponseStream
services.whatItDoes: Returns response tokens as a stream of chunks, allowing progressive text display as the model generates
whenToChoose: Users complain about long wait times
whenNotToChoose: Batch processing where full response is needed at once
commonTraps: Thinking a faster model solves progressive display -- without streaming, users still wait for the full response

services.name: Amazon Bedrock Converse API
services.whatItDoes: Model-agnostic interface with unified request/response format across all Bedrock models; supports tool use, streaming, and multi-turn conversations
whenToChoose: Unified API across Claude, Nova, Llama
whenNotToChoose: Single-model applications where InvokeModel is simpler
commonTraps: Building custom model abstraction layers when Converse API already provides this
Not knowing Converse API exists and using model-specific InvokeModel for each model

services.name: Bedrock Inference Profiles
services.whatItDoes: Configurable traffic routing between models with adjustable weights for canary/blue-green deployment patterns
commonTraps: Building ALB-based traffic splitting for Bedrock models when inference profiles provide this natively

services.name: Multimodal FMs
services.whatItDoes: Foundation models that natively accept both images and text, processing them together in a single API call
whenToChoose: Visual content analysis with text generation
whenNotToChoose: Pure image classification without text generation
commonTraps: Chaining Rekognition + text FM when a single multimodal call does both with less effort and better quality

categories.title: Evaluation Metrics: Which Metric When?
categories.subtitle: ROUGE, BLEU, MMLU, human evaluation, and bias detection

decisionPatterns.scenario: A team needs to measure how well their model's summaries capture the same information as human-written reference summaries.
decisionPatterns.why: Measures n-gram overlap between generated and reference text — the standard metric for summarization. BLEU is for translation, not summarization.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A company is choosing between three FMs for a reasoning-heavy application and needs standardized benchmarks to compare general knowledge and logic.
decisionPatterns.why: Industry-standard benchmarks: MMLU tests knowledge breadth, HellaSwag tests common-sense reasoning, ARC tests science reasoning. BLEU/ROUGE measure text similarity, not reasoning.

decisionPatterns.scenario: Automated metrics score 0.9+ but the marketing director says the AI copy 'reads like a Wikipedia article' — it lacks brand personality and emotional hooks.
decisionPatterns.why: Brand voice, emotional appeal, and creative tone are subjective qualities no automated metric can capture. Domain experts rate outputs on custom rubrics. Supplements, not replaces, automated metrics.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A loan summary generator uses subtly different language for different demographic groups with identical financial profiles — the team needs to address this bias.
decisionPatterns.why: Always quantify bias before trying to fix it. Clarify provides measurable fairness metrics across groups. Without a baseline, you can't tell if your mitigation actually helped.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A GenAI app's quality has been gradually declining for two months even though nothing in the code or model has changed.
decisionPatterns.why: Real-world query patterns shifted while the model stayed static. Periodic evaluation against updated test datasets detects this concept drift. CloudWatch only shows infrastructure health.

services.name: ROUGE
services.whatItDoes: Measures n-gram overlap, longest common subsequences, and word pairs between generated and reference text -- the standard metric for summarization
commonTraps: Using ROUGE for translation tasks (that's BLEU)
Expecting ROUGE to capture semantic quality (it measures surface overlap)

services.name: MMLU / HellaSwag / ARC
services.whatItDoes: Standard FM benchmarks: MMLU tests knowledge across 57 subjects, HellaSwag tests common-sense reasoning, ARC tests science reasoning
commonTraps: Confusing text similarity metrics (BLEU/ROUGE) with reasoning benchmarks (MMLU/ARC)

services.name: Human Evaluation (Bedrock Model Evaluation)
services.whatItDoes: Domain experts rate model outputs on custom qualitative criteria (brand voice, creativity, tone, emotional appeal) using Bedrock's human evaluation workflow
whenToChoose: Automated metrics don't capture stakeholder concerns
examKeywords: automated metrics high but quality low
commonTraps: Trying to solve subjective quality problems with better automated metrics
Optimizing model for metrics that don't align with business requirements

services.name: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
services.whatItDoes: Detects and quantifies bias in model outputs across demographic groups using statistical fairness metrics
whenToChoose: Bias detected or suspected in outputs
commonTraps: Jumping to mitigation (removing data, switching models) before measuring the bias -- always measure FIRST

categories.title: Responsible AI Features
categories.subtitle: Watermarking, source lineage, bias detection, and AI transparency

decisionPatterns.scenario: A news org wants readers and other platforms to be able to verify whether an image was AI-generated, even if someone crops or resizes it.
decisionPatterns.why: Embeds imperceptible markers in AI-generated images that survive modifications. Machine-verifiable — unlike text disclaimers, which are easily removed and not detectable by tools.

decisionPatterns.scenario: Regulators need to audit which source documents were used to generate each AI output to verify the credibility of the information.
decisionPatterns.service: Output Metadata Tagging + Glue Data Catalog
decisionPatterns.why: Tagging outputs with source references creates content-to-source traceability. Glue Data Catalog provides a searchable inventory of all source datasets. CloudTrail tracks API calls, not content lineage.

decisionPatterns.scenario: An audit reveals a model produces subtly biased language across demographic groups — the team needs to know the first step before implementing any fix.
decisionPatterns.why: You can't fix what you haven't measured. Clarify quantifies the bias with statistical metrics, establishing a baseline so you can prove your mitigation actually reduced it.

services.name: Bedrock Watermarking
services.whatItDoes: Embeds imperceptible markers in AI-generated images that persist through modifications and can be detected by verification tools
commonTraps: Thinking text disclaimers provide verifiable provenance -- they're easily removed and not machine-readable

services.name: Source Lineage (Metadata Tagging + Glue Data Catalog)
services.whatItDoes: Tags model outputs with source document references and maintains a searchable inventory of all source datasets
whenToChoose: Need to trace outputs back to source data
whenNotToChoose: Simple content generation without sourcing requirements
commonTraps: Choosing CloudTrail for source lineage -- CloudTrail tracks API calls, not content-to-source relationships

categories.title: Prompt Management & Engineering
categories.subtitle: Prompt versioning, Prompt Management service, and prompt lifecycle

decisionPatterns.scenario: A team manages 30 prompts across 5 apps and needs version control, instant rollback when a new prompt causes regressions, and a single source of truth.
decisionPatterns.why: Centralized prompt versioning with ARN-based references. Apps point to a prompt ARN — switching versions is instant, no redeployment needed. Git+CI/CD adds unnecessary deployment overhead for prompt-only changes.

decisionPatterns.scenario: A cross-functional team wants to accelerate their GenAI development workflow — auto-generating code, running tests in CI/CD, and getting real-time optimization suggestions.
decisionPatterns.why: Use Q Developer proactively for continuous code generation, test automation in CI/CD, and real-time refactoring. Using it only at merge time or for retrospective analysis underutilizes its capabilities.

services.name: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
services.whatItDoes: Centralized service for creating, versioning, and managing prompts with ARN-based references and instant version switching
whenToChoose: Need prompt version control and rollback
commonTraps: Storing prompts in environment variables (no versioning, requires redeployment)
Using S3 versioning for prompts (generic storage, no prompt-specific features)

services.name: Amazon Q Developer
services.whatItDoes: AI-powered IDE assistant for code generation, refactoring, test generation, security analysis, and performance optimization
whenNotToChoose: When manual review bottlenecks are required
commonTraps: Using Q Developer only reactively (at merge time) instead of proactively (continuous code gen + testing)
